Series::beta¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::beta(double other) const
Series Series::betaln(double other) const

What It Does¶

beta() computes the beta function B(a, b) elementwise, and betaln() computes its natural log. self supplies a; the argument supplies b:

B(a, b) = Gamma(a) * Gamma(b) / Gamma(a + b)
betaln(a, b) = lgamma(a) + lgamma(b) - lgamma(a + b)

The beta function is the normalizing constant of the Beta distribution and the value of the Euler integral integral_0^1 t^(a-1) (1 - t)^(b-1) dt. It appears in the Beta and Dirichlet densities, in the binomial coefficient (1 / ((n + 1) B(n - k + 1, k + 1))), and in the t and F distribution normalizers.

betaln() is the form to prefer when the result will be multiplied into a likelihood or other product. The implementation combines three lgamma values, avoiding construction of the enormous intermediate gamma factors. beta() is exp(betaln()); it is convenient when the bare normalizer is needed, but can underflow to zero even while the finite logarithm remains useful.

Properties:

  • Symmetric: B(a, b) = B(b, a).

  • B(1, 1) = 1; B(a, 1) = 1/a.

  • B(a, b) > 0 for a, b > 0; poles of the gamma factors at non-positive integer arguments propagate through.

Parameters¶

other (double): the second shape parameter b, a constant broadcast against every element of self.

Returns¶

Series beta() returns B(a, b); betaln() returns ln B(a, b). Same shape as self. An integral input is promoted to float64.

Gradient¶

Both forms are differentiable with respect to a (self). Because they are built from lgamma, whose derivative is digamma, the chain rule gives:

d/da betaln(a, b) = psi(a) - psi(a + b)
d/da beta(a, b)   = B(a, b) * ( psi(a) - psi(a + b) )

b is a constant double and carries no gradient. Where a gamma factor sits on a pole the sensitivity is NaN.

Examples¶

Example 1. B(2, 3) = 1/12; B(3, 3) = 1/30; B(1, 3) = 1/3.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0, 1.0}).beta(3.0)
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0833, 0.0333, 0.3333]

Example 2. betaln() is the log of the same values.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0, 1.0}).betaln(3.0)
) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-2.4849, -3.4012, -1.0986]

betaln(2, 3) = ln(1/12) = -2.4849.

Example 3. beta() is exp(betaln()), and both are symmetric in their arguments.

pluss::series::print(std::cout,
                     pluss::make_series({2.5}).betaln(4.0).exp()) << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout,
                     pluss::make_series({2.5}).beta(4.0)) << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout,
                     pluss::make_series({4.0}).beta(2.5)) << "\n";

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0277]
Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0277]
Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0277]

Example 4. The backward pass of betaln() is psi(a) - psi(a + b).

auto a = pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
a.betaln(3.0).sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.sensitivity());

auto aa = pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, aa.digamma().sub(aa.add(3.0).digamma()));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.0833, -0.6167]
Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.0833, -0.6167]

Example 5. The backward pass of beta() carries the extra B(a, b) factor.

auto a = pluss::make_series({2.0, 4.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
a.beta(3.0).sum().reverse();

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.0903, -0.0103]

B(2, 3) * (psi(2) - psi(5)) = (1/12) * (-1.0833) = -0.0903.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Reach for betaln() when accumulating log probabilities. beta() can underflow for large positive arguments where betaln() is still finite.

  • b is a constant and carries no gradient; only a does.

  • Non-positive integer values of a, b, or a + b land on gamma poles and propagate inf / NaN.

  • betaln() is lgamma(a) + lgamma(b) - lgamma(a + b) — a difference of logs, not the log of a difference.

Summary¶

beta(b) is B(a, b) = Gamma(a) Gamma(b) / Gamma(a + b) and betaln(b) its log, with a from self:

  • symmetric; B(a, 1) = 1/a

  • prefer betaln() — beta() is exp(betaln()) and loses range

  • differentiable in a: betaln backward is psi(a) - psi(a + b), beta backward multiplies that by B(a, b)

  • b carries no gradient

See Also¶

  • Series::lgamma: the building block; betaln is a combination of three lgamma calls.

  • Series::digamma: the gradient of betaln.

  • Series::mvlgamma: the matrix-argument generalization of the gamma normalizer.
